name: El Yunque National Forest
label: El Yunque Forest
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Torre Yokahú' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Torre de Yokahú' (way/311664005): middle (10 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/14175177: large area 'El Yunque National Forest' (89658 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: The only tropical rainforest in the US National Forest System.

text.description:
El Yunque is a tropical rainforest in the Sierra de Luquillo mountains, in the north-east of Puerto Rico. It is the only tropical rainforest in the US National Forest System, and the U.S. Forest Service has managed it since 1903. The Spanish Crown had already set the land aside in 1876 to protect its soil and water, which makes it one of the oldest forest reserves in the Western Hemisphere. Today it covers about 28,500 acres and gets roughly 1.2 million visitors a year.

For photographs, the easiest high viewpoint is Torre Yokahú, a tower beside the road. From the top you look out over the rainforest canopy, the mountains around it and, on clear days, the coastline and the ocean. Guides describe it as the easiest high viewpoint to reach, with a parking area close by and only a short climb up the stairs. The view is wide and layered, with green ridges fading into haze.

Two other viewpoints are worth knowing about if you are a keen walker. Torre Mount Britton gives a more rugged view with mist and cloud around the peaks, and Los Picachos gives a 360-degree view out to the eastern shore. Both need a hike, so they suit a longer day.

Cloud often hides the high points, so aim for a clear morning. Sunrise and sunset are the best times at the tower.
text.geographic_location: El Yunque National Forest lies in the Sierra de Luquillo in north-east Puerto Rico, mostly in the municipalities of Río Grande, Luquillo and Naguabo.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops near the forest. The tower is reached by road off PR-191, with a parking area nearby. San Juan is within about 40 km of the forest. Leave your vehicle in the parking area near Torre Yokahú, then climb the tower stairs to the top. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full sweep of canopy, ridges and sky. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single peak, a ridge in the mist or a stretch of coast.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Torre Yokahú (top of the tower, reached by its stairs off PR-191). A panoramic view over the rainforest canopy, the surrounding mountains and, on clear days, the coastline and the ocean.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line. Keep the tower rail out of the frame, or use it at one edge to give a sense of height. Try a slow panorama along the ridgeline, holding the phone upright and moving steadily. If you are fit and the trails are open, Torre Mount Britton and Los Picachos give higher, more dramatic views.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the green hills to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its detail. In misty conditions, a Live Photo can capture cloud moving across the peaks. Wipe your lens before shooting, as the air can be damp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or sunset at the tower. A clear morning is best, as the high points are often hidden by mist and cloud.

text.access_note: This is a national forest managed by the U.S. Forest Service, and some trails and viewpoints may close or change, so check the official site before you go for access and trail status.

name: La Coca Falls
label: La Coca Falls
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OSM W312214574 (La Coca): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
La Coca Falls is a waterfall in El Yunque, a rainforest setting where water, rock and thick green leaves fill the frame together. That mix suits a phone camera well. The white water gives a clear focal point, and the dark rock and bright foliage around it give the picture depth.

The falls are close enough to frame without zooming much. Start with the default lens (1x) and turn on the gridlines. Put the main drop on one of the vertical lines rather than dead centre, and leave a little foreground, such as leaves or rocks, to give a sense of depth.

If the view is tighter than you would like, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in more of the surrounding forest. If something is in the way, try the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out just the stream of water. Rainforest light can be uneven, with pale sky above and deep shade below, so tap on the water and slide the exposure down a touch to stop the white water turning into a blank patch. Wipe your lens first, as spray and humidity can leave a soft haze on the glass.

Take a few shots from the same place at different zoom levels, then pick the one that best shows the falls and the green around them.
text.geographic_location: La Coca Falls is inside El Yunque, in the rainforest setting that the map covers.
text.directions_text: No public transport is listed for this spot, so check the official El Yunque site for how to get there before you go, and for any access changes. The phone icon on the map is about 50 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole waterfall. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the forest around it, or the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to isolate the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 50 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the main drop of water on a vertical line instead of in the middle. Keep a little foreground, such as leaves, at the edge of the frame for depth. Keep the phone level so the rock edges don't tilt.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the water to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the white water keeps its detail. Try a Live Photo to catch the movement and pick the best frame afterwards. Wipe the lens first, as spray can blur it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even light, such as an overcast spell or when the falls are in shade, tends to keep the water and the leaves both looking natural. Harsh sun can create bright patches.

text.access_note: Access rules, any ticketing and the condition of paths in El Yunque can change, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Rainforest light can be uneven, with bright sky and deep shade in the same view.
Spray and humidity near a waterfall can leave a haze on a phone lens.
Overcast or shaded conditions tend to give more even light on waterfalls than harsh direct sun.
La Coca Falls is a waterfall within El Yunque.

name: Yokahú Tower
label: Yokahú Tower
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Yokahú Tower'.
notes: Stone observation tower with sweeping views over the rainforest and coast.

text.description:
Yokahú Tower is an observation tower in El Yunque National Forest on the island of Puerto Rico. It was built in 1963 by Frank H. Wadsworth, then Forest Supervisor and Director of the IITF. It stands 69 feet (21 metres) tall at about 1,575 feet (480 m) above sea level, and it is one of only two observation towers in the forest. The other is Mount Britton Tower, which sits higher and is often wrapped in cloud. Yokahú is generally thought to give the better view, and it is easier to reach because there is a car park close by.

For a phone photographer there are two good pictures here. The first is the tower itself: a tall, solid shape against green forest and sky. The second is the view from the top, if you can go up, with ridges of rainforest rolling away below you. Switch to the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to fit the whole structure in, and keep your phone level so the sides do not lean inwards too much. If the tower is open, take a second set of photos from the top using the default lens (1x) for the wide view and the telephoto lens for details in the valleys. Check the weather before you go, because cloud can hide the distance quickly.
text.geographic_location: Yokahú Tower is inside El Yunque National Forest, on the island of Puerto Rico. There is a car park nearby.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this spot, so plan to reach El Yunque National Forest by taxi or hired scooter from the nearest town or from your base in the area. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) for the whole tower from close range. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. If you climb the tower, the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for picking out ridges and treetops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Step back a little if there is room, and angle the phone upwards to catch the full height.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a vertical edge of the tower up with one of the lines to keep it straight. Leave some sky above the top. For the view from the platform, include a foreground edge of railing or tree canopy to give a sense of depth, and try a panorama across the forest if the air is clear.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the sky does not turn white. In misty conditions, tap on a distant ridge and nudge exposure up a little for a softer, clearer layer of hills.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check the sky and weather before you go, as a clear spell gives the best distant views.

text.access_note: Access and any rules about climbing the tower can change, so check the official El Yunque National Forest site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The platform at the top may be open to visitors, though this can change.

name: La Mina Falls
label: La Mina Falls
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Cascada La Mina' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Cascada La Mina' (node/4302863140): point.
pin_note: Position from OSM W513350723 (Río de la Mina): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Popular waterfall and swimming pool at the end of the La Mina Trail.

text.description: La Mina Falls is a waterfall that drops over boulders into a rocky pool, deep in the forest of El Yunque. It photographs well because the water, the dark stone and the green forest all fit into one frame, and the pool gives you somewhere to stand and look straight at the falls. From the rocks at the pool's edge, facing into the falls, the water fills the picture. This is the classic postcard angle. One walker's tip is to turn left just before the little bridge and make your way down to the water. Wear water shoes, because the rocks are slippery. Take care after rain, as flash floods are a risk here. Crowds can make a clean, people-free shot hard to get, so arriving early helps. For a second view, the bridge named for the Big Tree Trail and La Mina Trail shows the falls and pool from above and at a distance, framed by trees. The trailhead is the ranger station at Palo Colorado (Km 12.2, Road 191). The trail may be affected by hurricane damage, so check the latest notices on the day before you set out. Keep your phone in a pocket or a zipped bag while you scramble on wet rock, and take it out once you are standing safely.
text.geographic_location: La Mina Falls is on the Río de la Mina inside El Yunque, reached from the trailhead at the Palo Colorado ranger station. A bridge named for the Big Tree Trail and La Mina Trail gives a distant view of the falls.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops nearby. Head for the ranger station at Palo Colorado (Km 12.2, Road 191), which is the trailhead. From there, follow the trail down to the river and the falls. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fill the frame with the falls. If the pool is too tight to step back, try the ultra-wide (0.5x). From the bridge, use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick the falls out from the trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (base of the falls, on the rocks at the pool's edge, facing into the falls). The waterfall dropping over boulders into its pool, with the falls filling the frame. Pick a firm, flat rock and keep your feet steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the main drop on one of the vertical lines, with the pool along the bottom. Keep the camera level so the rock edges do not tilt. For a calmer, wider view, the bridge named for the Big Tree Trail and La Mina Trail shows the falls and pool framed by the trees from above.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the falls to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white water keeps its detail. Wipe the lens with a dry cloth before each shot, as spray and damp air blur it easily. Try a Live Photo or motion shot to catch the movement of the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning to noon, when the light is filtered through the leaves. Arriving early also helps with the crowds.

text.access_note: Trail status can change, so check the US Forest Service notices on the day before you go.

name: Mount Britton Tower
label: Britton Tower
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mount Britton Tower' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W311778946 (Mount Britton Tower): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Stone tower on Mount Britton with panoramic views.

text.description:
Mount Britton Tower is a small stone tower with a conical roof, standing in a clearing on a summit in El Yunque. It photographs well because it is the one man-made shape in a setting of palms and other trees, and the stonework is covered in orange lichen. That makes it look almost artificial against the greenery. It is free to visit, but you earn the picture on foot. The Mount Britton Trail is about 0.8 miles one way, with some steep sections, so allow time and take water.

The best phone photos are taken from the base of the tower, in the summit clearing. From there you can show the whole tower with the trees around it, then step closer for a second shot of the stone and lichen. Clouds often cover the summit, so an early start gives you a better chance of a clear background. Mist can also look good around the trees, but the sky may come out plain white. Keep the phone level so the walls don't lean. The top of the tower is a viewpoint rather than a place to photograph the tower itself, so shoot it from the ground.

Access can change: the road or tower may be closed for maintenance, or the reservation rules may have changed. Check the El Yunque National Forest alerts on the day before you set off.
text.geographic_location: Mount Britton Tower stands on a summit clearing inside El Yunque National Forest, at the top of the Mount Britton Trail.
text.directions_text: No stations or tram stops are listed for this spot, so check how to reach El Yunque National Forest before you go. From there, follow the Mount Britton Trail on foot to the summit clearing. The trail is about 0.8 miles one way, with some steep parts, and the tower is at the top. Check the forest alerts first, as the access road and tower have been reported closed at times. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the base of the tower. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you can't fit the whole tower and the trees around it. Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a close shot of the stone and lichen.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take the photo from outside the stone structure, at its base in the summit clearing, so the conical roof sits above you among the palms and trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so the walls stay straight. Take one wider shot with the palms and trees framing the tower, then move closer for a second shot of the orange lichen on the stone. If you use ultra-wide up close, keep the tower in the middle of the frame so it doesn't stretch at the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright and washes out. Lichen colours often look best when slightly underexposed. If the clouds are moving, take a Live Photo and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early, because clouds often cover the summit and an early start helps. A clear start gives you the best chance of a blue or bright sky behind the tower.

text.access_note: The tower is free and reached on foot, but the road and tower may be closed and a reservation may be needed, so check the El Yunque National Forest alerts on the day before you go.

name: El Yunque (Puerto Rico)
label: El Yunque Peak
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mt. Britton Tower' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Mt. Britton Spur' (roads).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/357266263: the OpenStreetMap point 'El Yunque'.
notes: The highest peak of the forest, often shrouded in clouds.

text.description: El Yunque is the famous peak of Puerto Rico's rainforest, a mountain the Taíno called Yukiyu. It stands in the middle of El Yunque National Forest, in the municipality of Río Grande, at just over 1,000 metres. It is the second-highest peak in the forest after El Toro, but it is the best known because of its shape and its cultural importance. The forest is also the rainiest of all US national forests, and the peak is nearly always wrapped in thin mist. That mist is what makes the photos moody, but it also means you should be ready for a blank grey sky. A good, quieter alternative to the summit is Mt. Britton Tower, on the way up, where you look out over the forest canopy and the coastline. If the weather is clear, the peak sits in the upper part of the frame. The tower is usually quieter than the summit. The old stone tower at the top is the classic shot, and Los Picachos nearby gives a 360-degree panorama. The trail is mostly paved but it is an uphill hike. Take a first shot as soon as you reach the tower, because the cloud can close in quickly. Then wait a few minutes and shoot again if the mist lifts. Check the current trail status before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the middle of El Yunque National Forest, in the municipality of Río Grande in north-eastern Puerto Rico. The peak stands immediately next to Los Picachos, and Mt. Britton Tower is on the trail below it.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops nearby, so you need a car. Drive from San Juan via PR 66 and PR 3 to the small town of Palmer, then follow PR 191 to its end, where a loop leads to the start of the Mt Britton trail. Parking there is very limited. Walk uphill along the trail to Mt. From there the peak is about 800 m to the north-east as the crow flies. The trail is uphill, so allow more time than a flat walk. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the view from the tower, then switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the peak. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the tower rail and the forest in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Mt. Britton Tower (on the Mt. Britton trail, reached by an uphill hike). A wide view over the forest and coastline from the tower, with El Yunque Peak in the upper part of the frame if the weather is clear. From the tower you look out over the forest and the coast, and the peak lies to the north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower third line. Keep the peak in the upper part of the frame and let the forest fill the rest. For a wide sweep, try panorama mode and move slowly. If you want a different view, the old stone tower at the summit and the platform at Los Picachos are the alternatives.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the forest to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright mist does not turn the picture grey. Wipe the lens before you shoot, as the air is damp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: A clear morning is best, because cloud and mist often hide the summit later in the day.

text.access_note: This is a National Forest trail, and parts of the route have been closed in recent years, so check the official site and current trail status before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The camera lens may fog or get damp in the humid forest air, so wiping it before shooting helps.
The mist can close in quickly, so it is worth taking a first shot as soon as you arrive.

name: Baño Grande
label: Baño Grande
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Baño Grande' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q111938261: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Historic stone swimming pool built in the 1930s by the Civilian Conservation Corps.

text.description: Baño Grande is a former swimming pool in the La Mina Recreational Area of El Yunque, built in the 1930s by the Civilian Conservation Corps. Today it is kept as a historic site and is looked after as a scenic spot, so the water is for looking at, not swimming. The best phone picture comes from the stone staircase that climbs up to the pool. Look back as you go and you can see the man-made falls pouring over the edge of the dam, with stonework and green forest around them. The pool is reinforced by a stone and masonry dam, and it is about 5.5 metres deep. It was designed by R.E. Pidgeon and H. Randolph, built between 1935 and 1938, and it was in use until 1968, when it was closed for safety reasons. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2017. It is also the larger of two CCC pools in the forest, about three times the size of the nearby Baño de Oro. Visitors often treat it as a quick photo stop, so you do not need long here. For a second picture, frame the pool itself with the stonework and trees, and the water spilling over the dam at the far end. Keep to the stone paths and do not go into the water. Parking is across the road at the Palo Colorado lot.
text.geographic_location: Baño Grande is in the La Mina Recreational Area, in the Palo Colorado section of El Yunque National Forest, in Río Grande. It is linked to the forest's trail network.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or similar stops serve this spot. Parking is across the road at the Palo Colorado lot. From there, follow the stone path to the stone staircase that climbs up to the pool. The phone icon on the map is on that staircase, so once you reach it you are in the right place. Check current access with the National Forest before you set off. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) on the staircase to show the steps, the falls and the forest together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole stonework and pool in one frame from the top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here, turn and look back to see the man-made falls pouring over the edge of the dam.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the falls on one of the lines, with a few stone steps in the lower part of the frame to lead the eye. For a second shot, continue up the staircase to the pool and frame it with stonework and forest, and the water spilling over the dam at the far end. Keep a safe distance from the edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the falls to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white water keeps its detail. Try a Live Photo to catch the movement of the water. Wipe the lens first, as forest air can be damp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even light under cloud or in the shade usually works well for water and wet stone. Check the weather before you go, as the area is rainforest.

text.access_note: The pool is a historic site open to the public as a scenic spot, but swimming is not allowed and parts of the forest can close, so check the official site before you go.
